label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Posting it today, first class, so it reaches Croydon before the 19th. Sign it with your own name where I've put [your name].

---

Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing. So here I am, a grown woman who has bought a stamp and stood in a queue at the post office like it's 1998. I hope you appreciate what I've been through for you. Read this on the train like you promised, not at your desk with the spreadsheet open behind it.

I'll start with the part you'll want to skip to: I'm not asking you to quit your job. I'm not asking you to sign anything or hand in any notice. I'm asking you to come with me to an open evening, on Thursday 19 November at 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. You'll sit in a room, listen to some people talk, eat whatever biscuits they put out, and go home. If it's rubbish, you will have lost one evening and I'll buy you food after. That's the whole ask.

Now let me tell you why I think you should.

Nine years, Kelechi. Nine years of checking other people's costings. You told me at my birthday that every day is the same spreadsheet, and you said it the way people say things they've said many times before, to many people, without expecting anything to change. I've been thinking about it since. You are a man who got an A in further maths and used to run unofficial tutorials in Moremi before exams. Half our hostel passed because you sat on a bed with a biro explaining things to people who had been too embarrassed to ask the lecturer. And now you spend your days making sure a contractor didn't round up the price of some bricks. I say this with love: you are wasting yourself.

You also said something on your last birthday that stuck with me. You said you just want to do something that matters before 40. You were a bit drunk and you said it quickly, but I don't think you were joking. You're 34. That's not a lot of runway, but it's enough.

Here is what's happening at my school. We have 1,100 kids in Peckham, and since September two of our Year 9 maths groups have been covered by a supply teacher. Not because anyone is bad, but because we can't find enough maths teachers, and that's true in half the schools in London. Those kids are getting someone different every few weeks or someone who doesn't know the subject well. Year 9 is exactly when some kids decide whether maths is for them or not. They need someone who makes it make sense.

And you do that. Remember Christmas, when you sat with my nephew and explained fractions using portions of jollof rice on plates? He still talks about it. He told me last week that "Uncle Kelechi made the rice into maths." You didn't have a lesson plan or a worksheet. You just looked at a small confused person and found a way in. That is most of the job, honestly. The rest is learning the tricks and getting used to the noise.

Let me tell you about last month. There's a Year 11 boy called Damola who had been stuck on simultaneous equations for three weeks. Three weeks of me explaining it three different ways and watching his face stay exactly the same. Then one afternoon it clicked, and he shouted "Is that all??" across the room, and the whole class clapped. Thirty teenagers clapping for simultaneous equations. I had to look at the whiteboard for a minute so nobody saw my face. I've had a good few moments like that over the years, and nothing in my life before teaching ever came close.

But you know I'm not going to lie to you, because you wouldn't believe the good bits if I did. So here are the bad bits.

Teaching is hard. Marking is endless. There are weekends where I'm sitting with a stack of books and a cold cup of tea and I'm asking myself why I do this. Some days the behaviour is real wahala, and you'll go home feeling like you were thrown in a washing machine. In my first term in 2019, I cried in the car park twice. Twice! I'm telling you because I want you to know it's normal, and because it did get better. Not all at once, but it did. By the second year I was a different person in that classroom.

The money is the other honest thing. The route I'm talking about is the salaried one, so you get paid while you train, which is a big deal. It's one year, and it would start in September 2027. But yes, your pay will drop in that first year compared to what you earn now, and I won't pretend otherwise. What you get in return is proper holidays, a pension, and a salary that goes up as you do. It's not a quantity surveyor's life, but it's a decent one. Have a look at the numbers at the open evening and do your own sums. You, of all people, will do them properly.

Now, the "I'm too old" speech, which I know is coming. You're not. There's a woman in my department who started at 41. She's one of the best teachers we have, and the kids are slightly terrified of her in a good way. Having done something else first doesn't count against you in a classroom. It's useful. You've worked with contractors, deadlines and difficult clients, so you already know a lot about dealing with people.

Here's what I think, and then I'll stop. You are patient. You are funny. You explain things without making anyone feel stupid, which is rarer than you'd think and which can't really be taught. Kids can tell within about ten minutes whether an adult respects them, and they would take one look at you and know. I can see you in front of a class, and it doesn't look strange to me at all.

I might be wrong. Maybe you'll go to the open evening and hate it, and decide that spreadsheets are your destiny after all. Fine. At least then you'll know, and you can stop moaning to me at birthdays about it. But I don't think you'll hate it, and I think you know that too, which is partly why you asked me to put it in writing.

So here is the plan. Thursday 19 November, 6pm, Lewisham. I'll meet you there, or we can go together from wherever suits you. You don't have to say anything or commit to anything. You just have to come and listen.

Text me yes or no. If it's no, I'll send you another letter. I have more stamps.

Your friend always,

[your name]

P.S. Applications for September open soon, so the timing is annoyingly good. I didn't plan that. I'm just saying.
